product_native.finding: The 50 ml eau de parfum uses a clear cylindrical glass bottle with a thick clear foot, rounded shoulder, dark matte cylindrical cap, pale liquid and a large off-white wrap label.
product_native.exception: The 500 ml format is a broad apothecary bottle with shoulders and a clear stopper rather than the small spray bottle.

product_native.finding: The label is an information object: scent name and number dominate; size and product form follow; ruled fields identify compound/label city, date, and recipient; black monospaced/typewriter-like text sits on warm off-white stock.
product_native.exception: Exact field wording varies by format and market.

product_native.finding: The core CMF is low-chroma and utilitarian: clear glass, pale amber liquid, charcoal/black closures, warm paper labels, black ink and kraft board; visible texture and small imperfections are retained.
Fine and home fragrances repeatedly use an ingredient/note word plus integer (SANTAL 33, ROSE 31, SANTAL 26); body care instead foregrounds format plus scent (SHOWER GEL / Hinoki).
product_native.exception: ANOTHER 13 is not a literal ingredient name; body/grooming and generic formats do not follow note-plus-number.

product_native.finding: The site treats the received package as formulation truth: full INCI appears on PDPs, with a warning that lists may change and the package list is most current.

The full Classic discovery object is 17 narrow 1.5 ml clear vials with black caps, aligned in two rows in a black die-cut insert inside a brown kraft hinged box; the outer package receives a personalized label.
Classic candles use high-dose fragrance oils, a custom wax blend, natural-fiber wicks and glass vessels, then enter the same kraft-box/personalized-label system.
product_native.exception: Concrete candles and other home formats exist and are not evidenced here as sharing the glass vessel.

product_native.finding: Body care uses task-native squeezable containers: a 250 ml easy-to-squeeze bottle for shower gel and a 55 ml easy-to-squeeze tube for hand pomade; copy emphasizes vegan ingredients, texture, action and scent.
The travel case is a heavy vintage metal tube protecting a 10 ml spray; its utilitarian form becomes personal through initials engraved on the lower back.

representation.finding: Hero product imagery isolates one object low and small within a square, grey low-key field, with directional shadow, muted reflections and extensive negative space; labels remain legible rather than retouched away.
Different sizes are represented as separate truthful container archetypes, not forced into one identical silhouette; the 500 ml decanter shows its stopper and bulk directly.
Personalization is represented as a manual event: two hands align a printed label over a bottle on a dark workbench, with tools and packaging present.
The discovery set is shown open in three-quarter view so the kraft shell, black insert, vial count and arrangement are simultaneously inspectable.
PDPs sequence object and transaction facts first (name, form, size, quantity, personalization, delivery/pickup), then an evocative scent narrative, then ingredients/safety and recommendations.
Representation makes administrative evidence (label, date, city, dosage/size, ingredients) part of luxury rather than hiding it behind decorative packaging.
representation.alternative: The label may primarily be a recognizable visual trademark, with information value secondary.
representation.falsifier: A broad current corpus showing most labels illegible, decorative-only, or absent.

service_behavior.finding: Product configuration exposes size and quantity plus a 23-character label/box message and a short engraving field; unpersonalized creations default to 'You', while personalized labels are final sale.
PDP fulfillment is market-aware: home delivery timing/thresholds, selected-market same-day or next-day delivery, and store pickup links appear beside the configuration flow.
service_behavior.exception: Thresholds and modes vary by locale.

service_behavior.finding: Discovery is a staged commitment service: 5- or 17-scent 1.5 ml sets enable exploration, while 17-scent sets bundled with a 50 ml or 100 ml gift card convert later choice into an online or in-store full bottle.

Online refill is reverse logistics: order the identical scent/size, receive a dedicated box with instructions and a surprise, cap and secure the empty bottle with invoice and supplied label, ship it back, then receive the refilled bottle in an indicated 5–10 business days.

Refill eligibility requires an empty, undamaged bottle and preserves identity: no scent or size changes. Online covers 50/100 ml; select labs additionally handle 500 ml and make the process an in-person experience.
service_behavior.exception: The live/cached FAQ disagrees by locale on whether Classic Collection is currently eligible online; contact confirmation is explicitly advised.

service_behavior.finding: Every refill is freshly blended by a lab technician and receives a new date label; personalization may change, otherwise the recipient reads 'You'. Freshly compounded perfume then macerates for typically at least 14 days, during which smell can evolve.
The refill program is framed as continuity ('same bottle, same scent, same perfume') at about 20% below retail, not as a different refill SKU experience.

Store discovery is operational: use the locator's refill icon, contact the lab to confirm scent and size, and choose store pickup, phone ordering, or in-person lab service. Changing shipping country empties the shopping bag.

claims.claim: Personalized production metadata is part of the physical product, not only gift wrapping.
claims.alternative: It could function mainly as gifting novelty.
claims.falsifier: Most standard orders ship without city/date/recipient labels.

claims.claim: The shared label system is a stronger family invariant than container silhouette.
claims.alternative: Kraft packaging may be equally or more invariant.
claims.exceptions: Body formats were not visually sampled at equal depth.
claims.falsifier: A complete current SKU audit finds label structure changes across most categories.

claims.claim: Sampling is an owned product ladder, not a complimentary afterthought.
claims.alternative: Gift-card bundles may be primarily gifting products.
claims.exceptions: Availability and set composition can change.
claims.falsifier: Discovery products disappear from navigation or cease being sold separately.

claims.claim: Refill turns wear, elapsed time and continued ownership into a repeat service ceremony.
claims.alternative: The main driver may be price or waste reduction rather than ceremony.
claims.exceptions: Only eligible bottles, sizes and participating labs qualify.
claims.falsifier: Refills move to anonymous bulk cartridges with no returned bottle, technician or dated relabeling.

claims.claim: The lab vocabulary joins retail, production and client care into one role system: stores are labs and staff are lab technicians who blend, label and refill.
claims.alternative: 'Lab' may be thematic naming layered onto conventional retail operations.
claims.exceptions: Not every retail point offers refill or visible blending.
claims.falsifier: Current operational documentation shows no technician-led preparation at any lab.

claims.claim: The current catalog visibly repeats note-plus-number names, but official reviewed pages do not explain what the number encodes.
claims.alternative: The number may encode formula ingredient count, formula identity, or simply a naming convention.
claims.exceptions: ANOTHER 13 and non-fragrance format names complicate a literal rule.
claims.falsifier: A first-party naming explainer explicitly defines the number.

claims.claim: Formulation truth is allowed to change and the package label outranks web copy for the latest ingredient/safety list.
claims.alternative: This is standard regulatory boilerplate rather than a brand-specific behavior.
claims.exceptions: It does not explain why or how formulas change.
claims.falsifier: The warning is removed and site lists are guaranteed to match all shipped lots.
